statement: In 142 healthy adults with little drug experience and no psychiatric history who took LSD and/or psilocybin in six placebo-controlled laboratory trials in Switzerland (Müller et al., 2022), 13 (9.2%) described flashback-like experiences when asked at the end of the study: 7 of 90 after LSD only, 2 of 24 after psilocybin only and 4 of 28 after both. They were mostly single, brief visual changes lasting seconds to minutes, mostly in the days right after the last session, and 10 of the 13 felt neutral or pleasant; 2 people (1.4%) found them distressing, one of whom went on to have panic attacks and left the study, and one person had brief visual flashbacks, which she felt as positive, on and off for seven months. No one reported problems in daily life and no one was found to meet the criteria for hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD); with no case among 142 people, a true rate of up to about 2% cannot be ruled out (editors' calculation). There was no comparison with how often similar experiences happen without a drug, and the participants were screened volunteers, so rates in recreational use may differ. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: About 1 in 11 healthy volunteers who took LSD or psilocybin in lab studies said they later had a flashback, usually a short change in what they saw, in the days after. Most did not mind it; 2 of 142 were upset by it. Nobody developed lasting vision problems. These were careful lab studies with screened people, so it may be different in everyday use.
population: Healthy adults aged 25 to 65 with little previous drug use and no personal or family psychiatric history, in six placebo-controlled crossover trials in Basel (142 people, 74 women)
exposure: LSD and/or psilocybin given in the trials
comparator: None for the flashback outcome (frequencies are descriptive)
outcome: Flashback phenomena reported at the end-of-study visit and at follow-up; DSM-5 hallucinogen persisting perception disorder
magnitude: 13 of 142 (9.2%): LSD only 7 of 90 (7.8%), psilocybin only 2 of 24 (8.3%), both 4 of 28 (14.3%); distressing 2 of 142 (1.4%); HPPD 0 of 142 (editors' calculation: one-sided 95% upper limit about 2.1%). Mostly visual (11 of 13), seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%); single occurrence in 53.8%.

statement: In 24 healthy adults with previous LSD experience given a single low laboratory dose of LSD and, on another day, a placebo (one randomized, double-blind crossover study in Brazil; Wiessner et al., 2022), the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD changes thinking the next morning. In models adjusted for body mass index and time since last psychedelic use, people recalled a complex drawing and card locations somewhat better and named more words beginning with a given letter after LSD than after placebo, but did worse on a card-sorting test of mental flexibility (fewer categories completed, more errors and repeated wrong answers), with partial eta squared from 0.19 to 0.34; attention, self-control, reasoning, word-list memory and drawing fluency did not differ. About 66 test scores were analysed without correction for multiple testing, the authors report that the unadjusted analyses showed few differences, practice effects were large, the paper's text and table disagree on the direction of two card-sorting scores, and a few people account for much of the card-sorting difference in the figure. The study did not measure mood or sleep. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Twenty-four people who had taken LSD before took a small dose in a lab, and a dummy drink on another day. The next morning they did memory, word and puzzle tests. After LSD, a few memory and word scores were a little better and one card-sorting puzzle was a little worse than after the dummy drink. These small differences may be chance, because many scores were checked. Mood and sleep were not measured.

exposure: A single low oral dose of LSD given by researchers in the morning (amount and timing are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people after an inactive placebo in a separate session two weeks apart
outcome: Performance on memory, fluency, mental flexibility, attention, inhibition and reasoning tests the next morning

statement: In 213 healthy volunteers aged 25 to 64 (108 women) who took LSD mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present (some sessions included an MRI scan), and placebo on another day in eight of the nine studies (nine double-blind crossover studies pooled by the Basel laboratory that ran them, 297 LSD sessions; one dose by mouth per session, 25 to 200 micrograms, as study conditions; Vizeli et al., 2024), the dose given was the strongest predictor of almost every effect compared with placebo, and characteristics measured before the dose were also associated with the response at a given dose: higher well-being rated just before, with stronger subjective effects in general, by the Discussion's summary (it was significantly associated with every self-rated scale, the anxiety-type scales included, except a bad drug effect and two others; the direction scale by scale is shown only in a figure not read); anxiety rated just before, with more anxiety during the session; openness, with more mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion, with more visual and auditory changes; more previous hallucinogen experience, with a smaller overall altered state and less anxious ego dissolution; and genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6, with higher blood levels of LSD and more anxious ego dissolution. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness showed no significant association with any effect. Older age went with more, and higher body weight with less, bad drug effect, and women had smaller increases than men in four positive ratings and in body temperature; women's slightly less positive ratings were not significant when one dose per study was analysed (the text does not say whether the temperature difference held), and the abstract's statement that sex and body weight had no significant influence does not match the main results. The text gives the direction and significance of each association after correction for 551 tests but no sizes, which are only in a figure and a supplement not read here, so how much any characteristic other than dose matters cannot be said; bad drug effects were generally small. Expectations were not among the 19 predictors, and the setting barely varied. Genes for the CYP2D6 enzyme and earlier hallucinogen use went with feeling more or less from the same amount; earlier use was compared between people, so it cannot show that use itself changed the response. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy adults, the LSD dose was linked most closely to how strong the effects were. People who felt well just before had stronger effects, people who felt anxious had more anxiety, open personalities had more mystical feelings, and people who had used hallucinogens more often had a smaller overall effect. The paper gives the direction of each link but not its size. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

exposure: Characteristics measured before dosing: dose, mood just before the dose, personality, previous hallucinogen experience, CYP2D6 genetic activity score, age, sex and body weight; whether the session included an MRI scan
comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at a given dose (placebo sessions in the same people in eight of nine studies)
outcome: Self-rated effects relative to placebo (visual analogue scales, 5D-ASC, MEQ30), blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and blood LSD level
magnitude: Directions and corrected significance only; no sizes in the text. Dose strongest for every effect except body temperature (selected by LASSO for all 29 responses, largest for 21). Pre-drug well-being: significant for all subjective scales except bad drug effect, changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood, with effects more pronounced at higher well-being by the Discussion's summary; pre-drug anxiety: more 5D-ASC anxiety; openness: mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion: visual and auditory changes; previous hallucinogen experience: smaller 5D-ASC total, less anxious ego dissolution; lower CYP2D6 genetic activity score: higher plasma LSD and more anxious ego dissolution; age more and body weight less bad drug effect; women smaller increases in four positive ratings (not significant in the one-dose sensitivity analysis) and in temperature (not reported there).

statement: In people who had used LSD in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (13,769 respondents reported past-year use: 63.9% were under 25, 79.6% men, and most lived in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), 102 of the 10,293 who answered the question (1.0%; about 1 in 100, or 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after LSD in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (75% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 10,293 as the past-year group. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, nothing that was taken was tested, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 102 people by an estimated 53,627 days of use (a mean of 5.21 days a year), the authors put the figure at 0.2% of past-year uses, which they call an underestimate because each person is counted once. In the companion analysis of the same survey, 19 of 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after them, a share the authors describe as about five times lower (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). Saying yes was more common among people with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% against 0.7%; χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001), among younger people (median age 21 against 22; p = 0.003) and among those with more days of use in the past year (median 3 against 2; p = 0.029), in separate tests without adjustment, and it did not differ by sex or by first use in the past year. Of the 102, most ticked anxiety or panic (71) and confusion (66), and many paranoia (50) or seeing or hearing things (46); 21 (20.6%) ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm, 17 (16.7%) an accident or trauma, 13 (12.7%) seizures and 12 (11.8%) passing out, none of it verified, and the authors say it is unknown which symptoms came from LSD and which from other drugs taken. 54.5% said they had been admitted to hospital, a share the authors call surprising and print without a count, noting that the survey did not define admission. The paper gives recovery as percentages without a denominator, 59.2% back to normal within 24 hours and 11.2% with consequences lasting beyond 4 weeks; both fit 98 respondents, and the editors' reading of the figure, which prints no values, gives 58 of 98 back to normal within 24 hours, 40 taking longer, 17 not back to normal after 5 to 7 days and 11 with problems beyond 4 weeks, 6 of whom said they had not recovered (the abstract gives the 11). statement: In US adults living in households, surveyed in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health from 2001 to 2004 (130,152 respondents, a randomly selected sample representing the civilian adult population not living in institutions; response rate 78%, and about 10% more excluded from the public data file; Krebs & Johansen, 2013; funded by the Research Council of Norway, no competing interests declared), having ever used LSD, psilocybin (magic mushrooms), mescaline or peyote (21,967 people, 13.4% weighted; of them, 80.1% had used LSD, 61.5% psilocybin and 37.8% mescaline or peyote), compared with never having used any of them (108,034 people), is associated with higher unadjusted rates of each of 20 past-year mental health indicators but, after adjustment, with no higher odds of any of them. Before adjustment every indicator was more common in people who had used these drugs, by about 1.8 to 3.2 times (editors' calculation from the weighted percentages; for example serious psychological distress 15.5% against 7.5%, inpatient mental health treatment 2.9% against 0.9%, symptoms of a major depressive episode 6.8% against 2.7% and of non-affective psychosis 4.4% against 1.8%), and these people also differed on every other factor measured (for example lifetime cannabis use 98.2% against 33.0%, cocaine 70.1% against 6.7%, an extremely stressful event 52.3% against 33.9%). After adjustment for age, sex, ethnicity, income, education, marital status, liking to take risks, a lifetime extremely stressful event and lifetime use of ten other kinds of drugs, the adjusted odds ratios ranged from 0.7 to 1.1 (serious psychological distress 1.0, 95% CI 0.9 to 1.1; major depressive episode 1.0, 0.8 to 1.2; non-affective psychosis 0.8, 0.6 to 1.1; upper limits at most 1.6, for mania and agoraphobia), and none was higher for any of the drugs separately or for LSD use in the past year (1,220 people), although the past-year LSD estimates were imprecise (for example feeling a force inserting thoughts 1.7, 0.8 to 3.5). Some adjusted odds were lower (for example any of the drugs and feeling a force taking over the mind 0.7, 0.5 to 1.0; psilocybin and psychiatric medication 0.8, 0.7 to 0.9; LSD in the past year and serious psychological distress 0.7, 0.6 to 0.9), but no correction was made for the 120 adjusted estimates in the tables and the further stratified models (editors' count), and the authors say some weak associations are likely due to chance. Everything was self-reported in a private computer interview: drug use as ever having used, with no analysis of how often or how much, and mental health as screening questions about the past year (the treatment items included treatment for alcohol or drug problems). The survey asked once, with no measures from before people first used these drugs, so it cannot show whether they cause, prevent or do not affect mental health problems; in the editors' reading, the absence of a difference depends on adjusting for other drug use, stressful events and risk-taking, some of which may have followed psychedelic use; and people in prisons, hospitals or the military were not sampled. The authors' statement that their findings do not support flashbacks or hallucinogen persisting perception disorder rests, for visual symptoms, on one item, having seen a vision others could not in the past year (probably asked only in 2001 and 2002, so answered by about two thirds of the respondents; adjusted odds ratio 1.0, 0.7 to 1.3; for past-year LSD 1.3, 0.8 to 2.1), which cannot identify a rare lasting condition. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a big US survey of 130,152 adults from 2001 to 2004, the 21,967 who had ever used LSD, magic mushrooms (psilocybin), mescaline or peyote reported each of 20 kinds of mental health problems asked about roughly 2 to 3 times as often as people who had never used them. But they had also used far more other drugs, taken more risks and lived through more extremely stressful events; once these and other differences were taken into account, none of the 20 was more common, and a few were less common, which may be chance. Everything was self-reported, and the survey asked people once, so it cannot show whether these drugs cause, prevent or do nothing to mental health problems; its one question about seeing things others could not cannot rule out rare lasting vision problems.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_krebs_2013 (ROBINS-E, first pass): overall high, from confounding, with some concerns for exposure, outcome, selection of participants and selection of the reported result. The adjusted estimates depend on the covariates: rates 1.8 to 3.2 times higher before adjustment became adjusted odds ratios of 0.7 to 1.1 after adjustment for other drug use, risk-taking, stressful events and background, some of which may have followed psychedelic use (over-adjustment), while mental health before first use and family history were not measured (residual confounding); either could move the estimates materially, in a direction that cannot be known. Exposure is self-reported ever-use and outcomes are self-reported screening items; household sample with 78% response, about 10% removed from the public-use file and institutions not sampled.

inconsistency.note: One survey; not assessable. Two later population studies listed by title on the card were not read.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: worded for US household adults in 2001 to 2004, lifetime ever-use and past-year screening items, not for recent, frequent or heavy use, for any one person, or for other countries or years.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: 21,967 people with lifetime use, and for any use every upper 95% limit is at most 1.6. The past-year LSD estimates are wide, and the statement says so.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; secondary analysis of a public data set without a registered protocol.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (one cross-sectional survey) starts low; down one level for risk of bias: very low. Rated as worded, an association in the US household population of 2001 to 2004: higher unadjusted rates, and no higher adjusted odds. Risk of bias is rated down because the adjusted result depends on which covariates are included, some covariates may have followed psychedelic use, and mental health before first use and family history were not measured, so the true association could be higher or lower than the adjusted estimates; self-reported ever-use and screening items add error. Not rated down for imprecision: for any use the intervals exclude increases above 1.6, although the past-year LSD estimates are wide. statement: In people studied from 1967 to 1970, both people given pharmaceutical LSD in medical or research settings and people who reported taking LSD outside them, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD, compared with no LSD or with each person's own sample from before LSD, changes chromosome breakage. Six of the primary studies have been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), among them the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage after LSD; the others, including the later and larger studies of those two laboratories and the study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968), are known only through one 1971 narrative review in Science (Dishotsky et al., 1971; figures second-hand; no search method or selection criteria stated; supported in part by the State of California Department of Mental Hygiene and by Mendocino State Hospital, where two of the authors worked; its tables include the authors' own unpublished study, and its second author, W. D. Loughman, was the first author of one of the negative studies, Loughman et al., 1967). What these studies measured was breaks seen under a microscope in chromosomes of white blood cells taken from the blood and made to divide in a culture dish, counted as breaks per cell in some studies and as the share of cells with any aberration in others, in groups of 1 to 46 people, by laboratories whose breakage rates in unexposed controls ranged from 0% to 11.9%; most breaks recorded were of a kind that the review's authors say mostly arises from the culture procedure itself, and they limit their own conclusion to damage detectable by the methods then available. The concern began with Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), as Tjio et al. (1969) note, mainly a study of cells in a dish, not of people: LSD added to cultured white blood cells from two donors, whose results were pooled, was followed by 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 conditions of concentration and exposure time, against 0.037 (34 breaks in 925 cells) in untreated cultures from six people, with no statistical test of the difference (the review nonetheless lists it as significant) and, in the paper's own Table 1, no steady rise with concentration; its one patient, a man given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy who had also been treated with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, had 12% breakage in 200 cells 8 months after his last session, against the 3.7% of untreated cultures from other people, with no sample from before LSD (the same laboratory's later report lists, as its case 37, a man of 52 who had taken LSD 15 times, the last 8 months before sampling, with phenothiazines as his only other drug and 39 breaks in 300 cells; he matches this patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, but neither paper says whether he is the same man). Later in 1967 the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage, both read in full, compared people who had taken LSD with people who had not, with coded slides but no samples from before LSD and no statistical comparison of the groups in either paper. Irwin and Egozcue (1967) found on average 23.6 breaks per 100 cells in 8 men who reported taking LSD an estimated 4 to 200 times (its source not stated; some had also taken cannabis, mescaline or peyote, psilocybin or DMT, not counted) against 11.9 in 9 volunteers who had not taken it (editors' calculation; 95% interval of the difference about 3.7 to 19.7), with overlapping ranges, no women in the LSD group, and the two highest control rates in people with x-ray exposure. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) found 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD, every one of whom had also taken other drugs or medicines (amphetamines 15, phenothiazines 10) and whose recruitment and source of LSD are not described, against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 controls without drugs, after two controls with 31.0 and 14.0 were left out for a viral illness that began within a day of sampling (5.4 breaks per 100 cells with them, pooled; 6.5 as the mean of the 14 controls' rates); yet 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (three of them chlorpromazine, two of them boys aged 9) had similar rates, 12.6 on average, no different from the LSD patients (editors' calculation; the paper makes no such comparison); and 4 children exposed to LSD before birth had 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults. Two other small cross-sectional studies found no excess: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people who reported heavy recent use of illicit LSD (7 of them also amphetamines), scored by someone who did not know their drug histories, against none in 112 cells from one concurrent control and 1 in 561 cells from 18 earlier controls of the same laboratory (Loughman et al., 1967); and 2.2 breaks per 100 cells (21 in 937) in 4 psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and 1.5 (14 in 914) in 4 patients given LSD in treatment, against 1.6 (15 in 950) in 4 hospital volunteers, with each sample cultured in two laboratories and blinding of the scorers not reported (Sparkes et al., 1968); groups this small cannot exclude a modest rise. The strongest study, Tjio et al. (1969), sampled 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis before and 1 to 10 days after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with coded samples scored by one reader who did not know whether a sample came before or after LSD: the share of cells with chromosome aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not a significant change (P = 0.3; 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 percentage points, editors' calculation); 3 patients had large rises (to 23.08%, 43.92% and 14.16%), and the 2 of them who could be retested were back within the normal range 71 and 229 days later (one still 2.32 points above his own earlier rate); there was no untreated comparison group, and 31 of the 32 had been given other medicines in hospital before their first sample. Cohen, Marinello, et al. and Tjio et al. both used LSD supplied by Sandoz Pharmaceuticals. What these designs can show is limited: cells in a dish are not people, blood cells are not sperm or egg cells (none of these studies examined those), and pharmaceutical LSD given in hospital is not street LSD of unknown content. In the review's tallies, of 310 people in 21 reports from 17 laboratories, at most 18 of 126 given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%) had breakage above their control group's average (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient is counted among the first; if he is also Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s case 37, he is counted among the second as well). The early reports of raised breakage in people, from 1967 on, came from three teams studying people who used many illicit drugs (80 of 86 people studied by two of them had raised rates; the first report of each is read, as above, the later ones are not), whereas nine other teams studying similar people (88 people, editors' sum from Table 2, including those of Loughman et al. and Sparkes et al.) found none beyond that in the general population apart from one infant exposed before birth; nearly all of these people used other drugs too (of 77 with raised rates and detailed drug histories, 43 had used amphetamine), Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had rates similar to their LSD patients (above), whom the review counts as exposed to illicit LSD although the paper does not say where their LSD came from, and only 54% of 57 street samples sold as LSD contained it in relatively pure form. In the editors' reading, the review authors' closing statement that they believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man goes beyond this evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: The LSD chromosome scare began in 1967 with a lab test: LSD was added to dishes of white blood cells from two people, with no check of whether the rise could be chance, and one patient who had also taken other medicines had more breaks, with no test from before LSD. Later that year, two small studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD than in people who had not: about 24 per 100 cells against 12 (8 people against 9), and 13 against 4 (18 patients against 12). Nobody had been tested before LSD, and in the second study every patient had also taken other drugs or medicines; there, 6 patients on other drugs or medicines but no LSD had about as many breaks as those who had taken it. Two other small studies of people who had taken LSD (8 people in each) found no extra breaks compared with people who had not. The best study tested 32 hospital patients before and after one dose of pure LSD, with slides read blind: cells with damaged chromosomes went from about 4 in 100 to about 6 in 100, a change that could be chance; 3 patients had big jumps, and the 2 retested months later were back in the normal range. It had no group without LSD to compare with. A 1971 review put the raised breaks down mainly to early studies of people using street LSD and many other drugs, and street LSD often was not pure; nine other teams found no rise. All these tests looked at blood cells, not sperm or eggs, and only at breaks big enough to see under a microscope. In a dish, aspirin broke chromosomes about as much as LSD. The review found almost no research on cancer, no birth defects reported after pure LSD and mixed results in animals; its authors' belief that pure LSD causes neither cancer nor birth defects goes further than this evidence.
population: People whose blood cells were examined from 1967 to 1970. risk_of_bias.note: Primary studies read in full: Tjio et al. (1969), coded samples scored blind before and after one dose, but no untreated comparison group, other medicines in 31 of 32 patients and infections between samples (card sc_tjio_1969, ROBINS-I serious); Irwin and Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967), cross-sectional comparisons that found more breaks (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12), with coded slides but no samples from before LSD, recruitment not described, self-reported LSD of unstated source and no statistical comparison; the first with groups differing in sex and x-ray exposure and other hallucinogens uncounted (ROBINS-E high), the second with other drugs or medicines in every LSD patient, similar rates in its own patients taking other drugs without LSD and two controls with high rates left out after the fact (ROBINS-E very high); Loughman et al. (1967) and Sparkes et al. (1968), cross-sectional comparisons that found none, of 8 people against 19 controls and of 4 against 4, with groups differing in other drugs, age and psychiatric illness, illicit exposure self-reported and blinding of the scorers not reported in Sparkes et al. (ROBINS-E high); Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors with no statistical test, and one patient without a sample from before LSD (editors' checklist, high). The later studies that reported raised breakage in groups of people are known only through the narrative review (card sc_dishotsky_1971: no search method or selection criteria; unpublished data, including the authors' own; its second author led Loughman et al., 1967) and cannot be appraised; as the review describes them they were small, with nearly universal use of other drugs, laboratories differing in methods, thresholds and control rates (0% to 11.9%), and no account of whether scorers knew which samples were exposed; one widely deviant value was excluded from a negative group.

inconsistency.note: Three teams reported raised breakage in people who used LSD and many other drugs, two of them in first reports now read in full (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), and LSD given into a vein raised it for a time in 3 people (as the review describes it), whereas the other studies read in full found no excess (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969, with 3 large rises among 32 patients), and most other teams in the review found none either. The explanation offered (other drugs and medicines, contaminated street drugs, infections, malnutrition, culture methods and high control rates) is plausible, and one paper read first-hand bears it out in part: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had rates similar to 18 LSD patients (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); but that comparison rests on 6 people, mostly taking prescribed medicines, and the rest on the review's account and its authors' impressions.

indirectness.note: Breaks seen under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture stand in for genetic harm in people; blood cells are not sperm or egg cells, which none of these studies examined (Tjio et al., 1969, p. 855); the cell studies (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967, and part of Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967) are not studies of people; children exposed before birth were compared with adults; hospital patients given pharmaceutical LSD, nearly all after other medicines, differ from people taking street LSD of unknown content; methods of 1967 to 1970; apart from the first two, the studies that reported raised breakage in people are seen only second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: Groups of 4 to 32 people in the primary studies read (1 to 46 in the review); in the largest study the 95% interval of the change, about −1.3 to +4.6 points from a starting 4.28% (editors' calculation from Tjio et al.'s Table 2), includes no change and a rise to about double; with 4 people per group only groups that do not overlap at all can differ significantly (Sparkes et al., 1968); the two studies that found an excess compared 8 with 9 and 18 with 12 people and reported no test (editors' 95% intervals of the differences 3.7 to 19.7 and 6.2 to 12.3 breaks per 100 cells), and the comparison that could separate LSD from other drugs rests on 6 people (interval of the difference −7.3 to 6.1); the review's counts have no intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review itself includes unpublished data.

grade.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November because four of the primary studies had been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3); later that day the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage were read in full too (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), without a change of rating. The human primary studies are observational, four cross-sectional comparisons and one before-and-after study without an untreated group, and start low; the cell-culture studies are preclinical and can only be indirect for people (§5.4). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision (domain notes): very low, the floor; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down twice, with the same result. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither an increase in breakage after LSD nor its absence can be shown with precision (§6.1): in the strongest study the share of cells with aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not significantly, with a 95% interval of the change (about −1.3 to +4.6 points, editors' calculation) that includes no change and a rise to about double, and 3 of 32 patients had large rises, back within the normal range in the 2 retested; the two cross-sectional studies that found no excess (8 people; groups of 4) cannot exclude a modest rise; the two that found about two and three times the controls' break rates (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12) had no samples from before LSD, did not describe recruitment and reported no statistical comparison, and in the larger of them every LSD patient had taken other drugs or medicines and 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so the excess cannot be attributed to LSD; and the cell studies reported no statistical test and no consistent concentration–response. Of the human studies that reported raised breakage, Irwin & Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) are now read in full; they leave the inconsistency and risk-of-bias judgments as they were, with the explanation of the positive findings now resting partly on first-hand data. The study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968) and the two laboratories' later studies enter only as the review describes them. The review is not independent of one negative study: its second author was the first author of Loughman et al. (1967), and its tables include the authors' own unpublished study. Where the review's figures differ from the primary papers, the primary papers are used: Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients and 5 volunteers, not 37 patients; one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate; the 5 volunteers' final average is 3.17% in the paper's own Table 4, not the printed 3.57% (editors' calculation); Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s cell study, which the review lists as significant, reports no test; Irwin and Egozcue print no group means, and their table gives 23.6 and 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation), not the review's 23.4% and 11.0% (11.9% in its table); Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say where their patients' LSD came from, report no test for their cells in a dish, and their Table 5 sums to 7735 treated cells, not 8725; and the review's statement that no positive study showed a relation with dose does not fit Irwin and Egozcue's own table, in which the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate in 8 people (editors' calculation). Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say whether their case 37, who matches Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s single patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, is the same man; if so, the review counts him both among people given pharmaceutical LSD and among people exposed to illicit LSD. The claim reports what was measured and where raised breakage was seen, so that a reader can see that the early reports came from people using many drugs and medicines and were not confirmed by the other teams; it does not adopt the review's closing statement that the authors believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man, which goes beyond the review's own findings that no significant work on cancer had been reported and that the human data on birth defects were case reports and one series. The cross-study tallies (14.29% against 48.9%) compare different laboratories and criteria and are not used as a rate ratio. Fly and animal findings are labelled and not used for people. Status mixed: the studies disagree, and the explanation offered for the positive findings (other drugs and medicines, street-drug contents, infections, culture methods) is plausible, and supported in one study by a small comparison group, but not established. The new anchors are not yet checked by a second reader, and studies after 1970 were not read and could change the claim. The statement gives no doses.

statement: In 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35; half had used a psychedelic before) who each took LSD (100 and 200 µg as labelled, in solution), psilocybin (15 and 30 mg, in capsules of the pure drug, not mushrooms) and a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in random, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions (study conditions), LSD compared with psilocybin made the effects last longer and raised heart rate more, while the higher psilocybin dose raised blood pressure and body temperature more; ratings of what the experience was like did not differ significantly between the higher psilocybin dose and either LSD dose on almost every scale, which in 28 people does not show that the experiences are the same (Holze et al., 2022). Length: from each person's 'any drug effect' ratings (a modelled curve, counted from and to 10% of the person's own peak), the effects lasted on average 5.6 hours (SD 2.2) after psilocybin 15 mg, 6.5 (2.4) after 30 mg, 9.3 (3.2) after LSD 100 µg and 11 (3.7) after 200 µg (both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses, p < 0.001); they began on average 0.4 to 0.6 hours after LSD and 0.8 hours after psilocybin, which the authors put down to LSD being a liquid and psilocybin a capsule, not to the drugs, and they say, without a formal test, that LSD's longer half-life in blood (about 4 hours, against about 2.5 for psilocin, the form psilocybin takes in the body) fully explains the longer duration. Kind: psilocybin 30 mg and either LSD dose did not differ significantly on any visual analogue scale or on any subscale of the main altered-states questionnaire (5D-ASC); LSD 200 µg was rated higher than psilocybin 30 mg only on 'ineffability' (how hard the experience was to put into words), and both LSD doses raised 'emotional excitation' on a mood scale more than psilocybin; the lower psilocybin dose gave lower peak ratings than the higher one on several scales. These are non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins, with most of the numbers in an online supplement that was not read, so the abstract's conclusion that the two drugs' effects do not differ beyond duration goes further than the tests can. Body: both drugs raised blood pressure, body temperature and pupil size against the dummy; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature significantly more than LSD, and both LSD doses raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses; on the group's average curves the differences were modest (systolic pressure roughly 139 mmHg after psilocybin 30 mg against 131 to 133 after LSD and 118 to 120 on the dummy over the same hours; temperature about 37.6 to 37.7 °C against 37.3 to 37.4 and about 36.7; heart rate about 76 to 82 beats a minute after LSD against about 72 after psilocybin 30 mg and 62 to 65 on the dummy over the same hours (its own early point, at half an hour, was about 69 to 70); editors' reading of the figure, as the peak values are in the unread supplement). Unwanted effects: total scores on a list of complaints in the first 12 hours rose with all four active conditions against the dummy, and from 12 to 24 hours with the higher dose of each drug; within 48 hours, counted by drug, 4 people had a headache after psilocybin and 3 after LSD, 2 had low mood after each, 2 and 1 had nausea, and there was one migraine (LSD) and one nosebleed (psilocybin), with 9 flashback episodes in 5 people within 72 hours (5 after LSD, 4 after psilocybin; what was counted is not explained) and no severe adverse event. Blinding: the dummy was recognised in 96% of sessions, and although the paper says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, by its own percentages people named the right drug (either dose) in at least 64% of psilocybin 15 mg sessions, 86% of psilocybin 30 mg sessions, 78% of LSD 100 µg sessions and 79% of LSD 200 µg sessions (editors' calculation: correct guesses plus guesses of the other dose of the same drug), so expectation may have shaped the ratings. How strongly people felt each condition varied widely from person to person (ranges in Table 1), and nobody took a second dose, so taking more was not tested. The study did not test which amounts of the two drugs match, and this answer gives none; the authors' figures on matching amounts rest on doses this study did not give. Three printed values for LSD 100 µg are impossible: two means in Table 1 and one in the pharmacokinetics paragraph lie outside their own ranges. The volunteers had little drug experience (at most 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs other than cannabis) and no personal or family history of major psychiatric illness, and were in a calm hospital room with an investigator; the LSD solution held about 15% less than its label (84.5 µg per 100 µg unit). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different? One careful lab study gave 28 healthy adults both LSD and psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms, each on separate hospital days along with a dummy, in random order and without telling them which. The clearest difference was length: LSD's effects lasted about 9 to 11 hours on average, psilocybin's about 6 to 7. LSD also started a little sooner, which the authors put down to it being given as a liquid. Psilocybin's higher dose raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more, while LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints such as headaches, and nobody had a serious problem. Otherwise, the trips were rated alike on almost every scale. But not finding a difference in 28 people does not prove there is none, and by the study's own figures people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. The study used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms, and did not test which amounts of the two drugs match.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the simple geometric visions seen on psychedelics come from spontaneous patterns of activity in the primary visual cortex (V1): a mathematical model proposes that they do, the paper tests it against no measurement in people on a drug (Bressloff et al., 2001), and no such test has been read for this answer. The model starts from Klüver's sorting of reported geometric hallucinations into four classes of 'form constants': gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; cobwebs; tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; and spirals. The paper says such images are seen after flickering light, certain anaesthetics, deep pressure on the eyeballs, on waking or falling asleep, and shortly after drugs such as LSD and marijuana, and, citing earlier reports, that they are also seen by blind people and in sealed dark rooms and keep their positions relative to each other as the eyes move, so that they arise in the brain rather than the eyes. The model rests on the map from retina to V1, which away from the centre of gaze works like a complex logarithm, so that circles in the visual field fall on V1 as vertical lines, rays as horizontal lines and logarithmic spirals as oblique lines, making tunnels, funnels and spirals simple stripes of activity across V1; and on the wiring of V1, with cells tuned to the orientation of edges, connections within each local patch, and long lateral connections that link patches of the same orientation preference along the axis of that preference, measured mainly in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews and scaled to human V1 (hypercolumns about 1.33 to 2 mm apart, about 1,300 per hemisphere); it extends an earlier model by the corresponding author and a colleague (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), which had no orientation tuning and could not produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, some chequer-boards or cobwebs. When the model's resting state is made unstable, by raising excitability or lowering inhibition, which the authors describe as thought to be one possible effect of hallucinogens, a limited set of repeating patterns can arise: with weak inhibition between neighbouring orientation patches, light-and-dark patterns that map back to tunnels, funnels and spirals, and with strong inhibition, lattices of oriented edges that map back to honeycombs, chequer-boards and cobwebs (elsewhere the paper lists chequer-boards among the light-and-dark patterns instead). Its limits: the drug appears only as an abstract excitability setting, with no receptor, drug or dose, and the same mechanism is offered for flickering light; the match with hallucinations was judged by eye against a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources; the contour-forming patterns that match seen form constants needed lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees from the orientation axis, wider than the anatomy that motivated the model, whose strict form gave patterns without continuous contours; the expected size of the patterns rests on an unsourced figure of 30 to 40 repetitions around the visual field (2.4 to 3.2 mm in V1); and some reported images, including a complex image after LSD, cannot be explained by the simple model, the authors say. The paper offers predictions, such as orientation changes detectable by optical imaging near the horizontal meridian, that it did not test. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Why do psychedelic visuals look like tunnels, spirals and honeycombs? A mathematical model suggests the visual brain's own wiring may shape them. The simple geometric visions people report, after LSD or cannabis but also with flickering light or on falling asleep, were sorted long ago into four types: lattices such as honeycombs and chequerboards, cobwebs, tunnels and funnels, and spirals. The wiring from the eye to the brain's first visual area turns a tunnel, a funnel or a spiral into simple stripes across that area. In the model, when the area becomes too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form on their own, shaped by how its cells are connected, and mapped back to what a person would see they look like all four types. But it is only a model: the drug is just an excitability setting, the wiring was measured mostly in animals, the match was judged by eye against a few drawings, the best-matching patterns needed wider connections than the anatomy it was built on, and some complex visions do not fit it. The paper did not test it against brain activity measured in people on a drug.
population: No participants: a mathematical model of human primary visual cortex (V1), built from anatomical and physiological findings in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews (partly unpublished, cited as personal communications) and from estimates of human V1 size and hypercolumn spacing, and compared with published drawings and descriptions of geometric hallucinations.
exposure: In the model, a rise in network excitability (stronger global coupling, or a steeper neural response through a steady input) or a fall in local inhibition, which the authors describe as one possible effect of hallucinogens and also apply to flickering light; no drug, receptor or dose is modelled.
comparator: The model's uniform resting state, and the earlier Ermentrout–Cowan model without orientation tuning; for the hallucinations, comparison by eye with a few drawings.
outcome: Which repeating (doubly periodic) patterns of V1 activity can emerge when the resting state becomes unstable, which of them are stable, and what they would look like in the visual field after an inverse retinocortical map; resemblance to Klüver's four classes of form constants, judged by eye.
magnitude: No statistical estimates. Retinocortical map constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 (estimated from Drasdo, 1977); orientation preference repeating about every 300 µm in cat V1 and 0.5 mm in macaque V1; 20% of lateral connections ending on inhibitory cells; human V1 about 3,500 mm² per hemisphere, hypercolumn spacing about 1.33–2 mm, about 1,300 hypercolumns; critical wavelength given as about 2.66 mm (2π × 0.400 / qc at qc = 1 gives 2.51 mm, editors' calculation); 30–40 repetitions around the visual field for commonly reported hallucinations (unsourced), corresponding to 2.4–3.2 mm in V1; contour-forming (even) patterns need lateral spread beyond 45 degrees (theta0 > π/4).
